status_summary: The record shows resizing of humanitarian funding and a partial shift toward faith-based partners, along with one step that differs from the Mandate's recommendation to move awards away from UN agencies. USAID closed on 2025-07-01 with more than 80 percent of its programs terminated (NPR), and the Rescissions Act (Public Law 119-28, 2025-07-24) rescinded $496 million of International Disaster Assistance and $800 million of Migration and Refugee Assistance. The FY2026 National Security, Department of State appropriations act, Division F of Public Law 119-75 (enacted 2026-02-03 per the Congressional Research Service), provides 5.50 billion dollars for two global humanitarian accounts: 5.40 billion for a new International Humanitarian Assistance account that carries the authorities of the former International Disaster Assistance and Migration and Refugee Assistance accounts, and 100 million for the Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance account. CRS states this is 25.8 percent below FY2025 enacted humanitarian assistance and above the Administration's request of 2.5 billion plus 1.5 billion dollars (37.5 percent higher than the request total). The U.S. Global Leadership Coalition, an advocacy group, reports roughly 37 percent below FY2025 using a broader set of accounts; its figure and CRS's were not reconciled. A supplemental request of 2026-06-24 sought a further 800 million dollars for the International Humanitarian Assistance account for Ebola response (CRS). On 2025-12-29 the United Nations and the US government signed a memorandum of understanding in Geneva under which the US commits $2 billion to UN-managed humanitarian funds covering 17 countries and the Central Emergency Response Fund (UN News); Capital FM reports the money moves through country-level pooled funds in place of project-based grants and stays open to UN and non-UN partners, and The New Humanitarian reports the US plans eventually to route all of its humanitarian funding through OCHA. On 2026-08-06 State announced nearly $2 billion for faith-based and community organizations, including $538 million for humanitarian response to Samaritan's Purse and a consortium led by World Vision and Compassion International (State's release was not reachable; DevelopmentAid republished it). On 2026-05-14 the UN Secretary-General's spokesperson welcomed an additional 1.8 billion dollars in U.S. humanitarian funding announced that day; the statement does not say how the money is routed or to whom it is awarded. No mission minimum for local partners, fixed-amount award policy, country exit strategies or explicit other-donor funding condition was found.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14169 paused foreign development assistance and required each program to be reviewed for consistency with US foreign policy (published 2025-01-30).
NPR reported USAID closed with more than 80% of its programs terminated and the remainder managed by State.

The Rescissions Act of 2025 rescinded $496 million of International Disaster Assistance, $800 million of Migration and Refugee Assistance, $57 million of Transition Initiatives and $43 million of the Complex Crises Fund.

The United Nations and the US government sign a memorandum of understanding in Geneva committing $2 billion to UN-managed humanitarian funds for 17 named countries (Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Ukraine, Haiti, Nigeria, Ethiopia, South Sudan, Mozambique, Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan, Bangladesh, Syria, Uganda, Kenya and Chad) and the Central Emergency Response Fund, per UN News; the Emergency Relief Coordinator says the deal does not mean agreement on every issue. Capital FM (via AllAfrica) reports the funds are country- and crisis-level pooled funds replacing earmarked project grants and stay open to UN and non-UN partners; The New Humanitarian reports the memorandum runs to 2027-12-31 with mutual exit clauses and that the US plans eventually to route all of its humanitarian funding through OCHA.

Congress approves the FY2026 National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs appropriations bill (House 217-214, Senate 71-29, per the Senate Appropriations Committee majority), enacted on 2026-02-03 as Division F of Public Law 119-75 (CRS). It provides 5.50 billion dollars for two global humanitarian accounts (5.40 billion for International Humanitarian Assistance and 100 million for Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance), 25.8 percent below FY2025 enacted and above the request of 2.5 billion plus 1.5 billion dollars, per CRS; USGLC reports different comparison figures.

The Spokesperson for the UN Secretary-General issues a statement welcoming a United States announcement that day of an additional 1.8 billion dollars for humanitarian work by the UN and its partners; the statement gives no routing or recipient detail.
timeline.source: United Nations, Spokesperson for the Secretary-General

timeline.event: The Administration transmits a supplemental funding request that includes 800 million dollars for the International Humanitarian Assistance account for Ebola response (CRS).

State announces nearly $2 billion in partnerships with faith-based and community organizations: $538 million for humanitarian response to Samaritan's Purse and a consortium led by World Vision and Compassion International (reaching a stated 7 million people in 16 crises), and about $1.4 billion for health services, including up to $850 million over five years to World Vision and a consortium of local faith-based implementers. State says at least 80 percent of health resources will reach frontline services.
